newsitem.title: UK: UK oil shares firm again on Middle-East tension.
newsitem.headline: UK oil shares firm again on Middle-East tension.

text.p: London oil shares climbed again on Tuesday after the U.S. launched strikes against targets in southern Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds in the north.

The attacks sparked an immediate response in the oil market with IPE gas oil and Brent crude futures expected to open sharply higher. IPE October Brent futures were up 51 cents at $22.50 a barrel on Simex down from a Gulf War high of $23.50.
Shares in Enterprise Oil added 6p to 527-1/2p, LASMO 2-1/2p to 198p, British Petroleum was up 3p at 635-1/2p and Shell 4p at 946-1/2p.

Iraqi military activity in the Kurdish north, prompted the United Nations over the weekend to put on hold a planned humanitarian Iraqi oil-for-food exchange and delay the first sales of Iraqi oil since the Gulf War six years ago.
That lifted oil prices and shares yesterday but the latest U.S. moves signal a marked escalation of the situation and is likely to delay further the return of Iraqi oil to the market.
With the rise in the political risk premium in the oil price, a rise in average 1996 oil price forecasts is unavoidable, said SG Strauss Turnbull analyst Irene Himona.

"The return of Iraqi oil is very unlikely in 1996. The oil market is going to enter winter with historically low commercial stock levels, the absence of 700,000 barrels per day of Iraqi oil and increased political tension in the Middle East region which all argues for a fairly tight oil market," said Himona.

However, the outlook for 1997 is clouded by political considerations and while the absence of Iraqi supplies may constrict the oil market to an extent, non-OPEC production is forecast to rise and expected to satisfy a significant proportion of 1997 oil demand increases.
"In addition, there are OPEC countries like Venezuela who are producing well above their quota and are actively trying to expand their productive capacity," said Himona.
"So there are supplies rising elsewhere and while the tight market may be in place over the winter the balance may start to change," she said.
